solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Architect's mood changed, questioning technique

indicators.note: letters that have been changed are put into a different order

parts.note: every letter of the phrase, the possessive S included

explanation.surface: A designer's temper has shifted, and someone asks how they intend to handle it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Socratic method is the philosopher's teaching approach of probing with a series of questions.

clue.text: Bloke, one with an axe?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an informal word for a man, a variant of fellow
second meaning: someone who fells trees

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second reading: a person who fells is literally one who cuts trees down with an axe.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is colloquial for a man or chap, and also names a woodcutter who chops down trees.

clue.text: Follow the rules and pass?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to cooperate and go along with what is required
second meaning: in a match, passing is literally moving the ball on to a teammate

explanation.surface: Advice to a footballer: stick to the laws of the game and give the ball away.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the literal sporting reading of the phrase, as opposed to its idiomatic sense of cooperating.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to comply or cooperate, and literally describes distributing the ball in a game.

clue.text: Artist with something to go on copper

parts.note: John is American slang for a toilet, something one goes on
copper is slang for a police officer

explanation.surface: A painter has something to work on, a sheet of copper perhaps, for an engraving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To go' is a euphemism for using the lavatory, so 'something to go on' is a toilet. John Constable was the English landscape painter of The Hay Wain.
explanation.definitionFit: John Constable was a celebrated English Romantic painter of landscapes.

clue.text: Plant: notice similarities when mentioned?

indicators.note: something mentioned is spoken, so we want a word that sounds like the one described

parts.note: to liken is to note similarities between things

explanation.surface: A botanist spots resemblances between specimens when they are pointed out.
explanation.definitionFit: Lichen is a crusty growth on rocks and trees, loosely treated as a plant though really a fungus-alga partnership.

clue.text: Aid dealing with very unlikely cure

parts.note: re means regarding or concerning

indicators.note: something unlikely is out of the normal order of things, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: so means very, as in so good
taken as written

explanation.surface: Help offered to someone pursuing a remedy that is very improbable.
explanation.definitionFit: A resource is a supply of help or support one can draw on, like an aid.

clue.text: Complete style for miss

parts.note: something over is finished
a look is a fashion style

explanation.surface: A total makeover suited to a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss' looks like a young woman in the surface; it is the verb meaning to fail to notice.
explanation.definitionFit: To overlook something is to fail to notice it, i.e. to miss it.

clue.text: Tenacious types, good in rows

indicators.note: one item sitting in another is enclosed by it

parts.note: tiers are rows set one above another
G is the standard abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Stubborn people sit well in their seating rows.
explanation.definitionFit: Tigers stands for fierce, persistent competitors who never give up, the animal used figuratively.

clue.text: Game seen by spotters, captor camouflaged

indicators.note: camouflage disguises the original appearance, so these letters are rearranged out of sight

parts.note: all the letters of the two words together

explanation.surface: A hunting game in which lookouts watch someone whose captor is disguised.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectator sport is one that draws crowds to watch, a game meant to be seen.

clue.text: Where God has come when daughter arrives immediately?

definitions.text: Where God has come when daughter arrives
definitions.meaning: first meaning, read literally: add D for daughter to the two-letter word for depart and the deity's name appears, so it originates in that word
second meaning: right from the very start

explanation.surface: A theological puzzle about where the divine originated once a girl was born.
explanation.walkthrough: D is the usual abbreviation for daughter. The question mark warns that the phrase is being taken literally in its first sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means from the very outset, straight away, so it can stand for immediately.

clue.text: Improve meeting

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to recover strength or pick up
second meaning: a mass gathering, as at a political event

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests making a meeting better, but the two words are separate senses of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for recovering or picking up, and a noun for a large public gathering.

clue.text: Old PM with European on top of the world?

parts.note: Lord North was British Prime Minister during the American War of Independence
a Pole is a person from Poland

explanation.surface: A former prime minister, accompanied by a continental ally, feels on top of the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On top of the world' suggests elation; the question mark warns it is meant geographically.
explanation.definitionFit: The North Pole is the northernmost point of the Earth, literally its top on a conventional globe.

clue.text: Big blow to Royal Navy, a trick

parts.note: taken as written
standard abbreviation
taken as written
to do someone is to swindle or trick them

explanation.surface: The fleet suffers a heavy setback through some deception.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big blow' reads as a setback for the Navy, but it is a violent wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A tornado is a violent rotating windstorm, literally a great blow of wind.

clue.text: Tall tower, where immaculate features are

indicators.note: something that features an item has it included inside

parts.note: in mint condition means perfect, unblemished
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tall tower in a place where spotless things are on display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Features' reads as a noun, but it is a verb: the word for immaculate features, i.e. holds, the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: A minaret is the tall slender tower of a mosque from which the call to prayer is given.

clue.text: Emperor of Romans seeking shelter, Carthage in ruins

indicators.note: something in ruins has been broken apart, so these letters are scattered and reassembled

parts.note: all the letters of the two words together

explanation.surface: A Roman ruler looks for refuge among the ruins of Carthage, the North African city Rome destroyed.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles the Great is the English form of Charlemagne, crowned Emperor of the Romans in 800.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlemagne was crowned Emperor of the Romans by the Pope on Christmas Day in the year 800.

clue.text: Sticking head in, so excited

indicators.note: excited things are agitated and stirred up, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: all the letters of the three words together

explanation.surface: Someone eagerly pokes their head into something, so thrilled are they.
explanation.definitionFit: Adhesion is the act or state of sticking firmly to something, the noun matching 'sticking' used as a noun.

clue.text: Soldier embracing military service ready — writing on the wall?

indicators.note: embracing something means holding it in one's arms, wrapped around

parts.note: GI is an American soldier
the Royal Air Force, a British military service
fit means ready or prepared, as in fit for action

explanation.surface: A trooper serving in the forces, prepared and seeing the omen of doom ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writing on the wall' is an idiom for an omen of disaster; the question mark tells you to take it literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Graffiti is literally words and drawings scrawled on walls in public places.

clue.text: Animal chained to rock

indicators.note: rocking shakes things about, so these letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: all the letters of the word

explanation.surface: A creature shackled to a boulder, like Prometheus in the myth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock' looks like a noun for the boulder; it is the verb meaning shake.
explanation.definitionFit: The echidna is the spiny egg-laying anteater of Australia and New Guinea.

clue.text: Stray yelped a lot

indicators.note: a stray wanders off course, so these letters are knocked out of place

parts.note: all the letters of the word

explanation.surface: A homeless dog barked over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stray' looks like the dog doing the yelping; it is a verb signalling that the next word is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Deeply means to a great extent, as in deeply moved, so it can stand for a lot.

clue.text: Why the whipping?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a punishment or scolding, as in to give someone this

explanation.surface: A puzzled victim asks why they are being flogged.
explanation.walkthrough: To give someone what-for is a British idiom for punishing or scolding them severely.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase asks the reason for something, and also names a severe punishment or telling-off.

clue.text: Ordinal in river, by the sound of it?

indicators.note: judging something by its sound means listening to how a word is pronounced

parts.note: the Forth is a Scottish river flowing into the Firth of Forth

explanation.surface: A query about the numbering of something positioned in a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Fourth is an ordinal number, indicating position four in a sequence.

clue.text: Student perhaps in residence, shout about site when one has left

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round the other

parts.note: to holler is to yell

indicators.note: one is the Roman numeral I, and its having left means that letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written, before its I is removed

explanation.surface: A residential student yells about the location of a site after someone moves out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' is the Roman numeral I, which is what leaves the site. 'Student perhaps' signals a definition by example: students are typical hostel residents.
explanation.definitionFit: A hosteller is someone who stays in a hostel, such as a student lodging in a hall of residence.

clue.text: Female behind dowdy type

parts.note: F is the standard abbreviation for female
the rump is the backside

explanation.surface: A woman trailing after an unfashionably dressed person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind' reads as a preposition, but it is the noun for the buttocks.
explanation.definitionFit: A frump is a woman who dresses in a dull, unfashionable way.

clue.text: Puppeteer ultimately prodding puppet in mocking manner

indicators.note: something prodding pokes into another thing, ending up inside it

parts.note: a dolly is a doll, a toy figure like a puppet

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the final letter is taken

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A puppeteer finally pokes their puppet in a teasing way.
explanation.definitionFit: Drolly means in a dryly amusing or wryly mocking way.

clue.text: Stirrer having a go with tart, I stirred!

indicators.note: things that are stirred are mixed about, so these letters are mixed

parts.note: the letters of a, go, tart and I; 'with' only joins them

explanation.surface: A cook boasts of having a try at making a tart and mixing it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition and the indicator are the same idea: an agitator stirs up trouble, and 'stirred' rearranges the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An agitator is a troublemaker who stirs up unrest, and also a device that stirs liquids.
